grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: To jest stolarz. Irena jest stolarzem. Nie jest właścicielką.

tables.caption: Jestem; jesteś; jest; jesteśmy; jesteście; są

grammar.note_en:
A predicate tells us something about a sentence’s subject. A predicate noun names who or what the subject is: a carpenter, a guest, a learner, a teacher or a resident. With a named person or a personal form of być (“to be”), these nouns take the instrumental case here. Irena jest stolarzem means “Irena is a carpenter”; Jestem gościem means “I am a guest”; Jan jest nauczycielem means “Jan is a teacher”. The instrumental does not mean “with” by itself. Earlier z Ireną meant “with Irena”; here stolarzem has no z and describes Irena’s occupation.

Keep naming and noun predicates distinct. To jest stolarz means “This is a carpenter”; Irena jest stolarzem means “Irena is a carpenter”. In the familiar to jest naming frame the noun is nominative, its naming form. With Irena as subject and a noun describing her role, stolarzem is instrumental. This is not a rule that every word after jest changes to instrumental. Stół jest czerwony means “The table is red”, with a nominative adjective; Lampa jest na stole means “The lamp is on the table”, with the already known locative place phrase. Łódź jest miastem means “Łódź is a city”: a noun predicate can describe a place as well as a person.

The demonstrated masculine instrumental forms are stolarz → stolarzem (“carpenter”), gość → gościem (“guest”), uczeń → uczniem (“male learner”), nauczyciel → nauczycielem (“male teacher”), właściciel → właścicielem (“male owner”), mieszkaniec → mieszkańcem (“resident”), and neuter miasto → miastem (“city”). Learn the complete spellings. Uczeń becomes uczniem, and mieszkaniec becomes mieszkańcem; do not simply append letters to their unchanged naming forms. The table collects actual forms already encountered, not a complete rule for all nouns.

Choosing a feminine noun and putting that noun into a case are separate steps. Właścicielka means a female owner; its instrumental is właścicielką. Uczennica means a female learner; its instrumental is uczennicą. Nauczycielka means a female teacher or instructor; its instrumental is nauczycielką. Their final -a changes to -ą. Do not turn masculine właściciel directly into właścicielką: that form belongs to the different noun właścicielka. Here the established word stolarz is used for Irena’s carpentry occupation, so its instrumental is stolarzem. The noun gość can also refer to Irena as a guest: grammatical noun gender is not a rule for changing the person’s sex.

Negation leaves this predicate instrumental in place: Nie jestem właścicielką means “I am not the female owner”. This is different from Nie mam lampy, “I do not have the lamp”, where lampy is a genitive direct object under negation. A role describing what someone is is not an object that the person has. Kim jesteś? means “What is your role?/Who are you?” in this context. Kim jest Irena? asks about her role. Kto jest stolarzem? means “Who is the carpenter?”: kto asks which person, while kim asks what role someone has.

Być has six present forms: ja jestem (“I am”), ty jesteś (“you are”, one familiar person), Irena jest (“Irena is”), my jesteśmy (“we are”), wy jesteście (“you are”, more than one person), and Ala i Ewa są (“Ala and Ewa are”). Polish often leaves the subject pronoun out when the verb form makes the speaker’s meaning clear. My and wy identify groups relative to the speaker: when Ala says my, she includes herself; when Irena says my in the next turn, she includes herself instead. The illustration keeps everyone in the same workshop while the speaker changes. The plural examples here describe static locations. They do not supply plural job-noun endings or the plural forms of other verbs.

Jan’s occupation and current task role are both true: Jestem nauczycielem, ale tu jestem uczniem means “I am a teacher, but here I am a learner”. Irena remains a carpenter; in this demonstration she is the temporary instructor. Ala is a learner in the task. A learner can be an adult with an occupation; no school enrolment, teaching subject or institution is stated. Zawód means “occupation”. The city/street sketch supplies the setting: w mieście is “in the city”, and w Łodzi is “in Łódź”. Residence in the city does not establish ownership of the workshop.

The separate SMS is a text message. Its written Jestem właścicielem (“I am the owner”) and Planuję wizytę w warsztacie (“I am planning a visit at the workshop”) belong to its absent sender. They do not describe Jan reading the words. Właściciel planuje wizytę means “The owner is planning a visit”. Planuję and planuje express present planning and take the noun wizytę, the accusative of wizyta (“visit”). No infinitive, motion verb or future tense is needed. The heading Warsztat identifies the property in question without teaching an ownership-genitive phrase. The owner has not arrived, and the lamp’s owner remains unknown. No earlier note, drawing or record is rewritten by this new message.
